Ising networks for binary data

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/ising-networks.Rmd
ising-networks.Rmd

Many psychological and educational variables are binary. A symptom may be present or absent, a diagnostic criterion may be met or not met, an assessment item may be passed or failed, and a behaviour may be reported or not reported. These variables represent distinct states rather than measurements along a continuous scale. Methods based on correlations and partial correlations among continuous variables are therefore not always appropriate. The Ising model provides a framework for estimating networks of binary variables (van Borkulo et al., 2014), and it is closely related to item response theory models, a link that connects the network and latent-variable views of the same data (Marsman et al., 2018). In an Ising network, each edge represents a conditional association on the log-odds scale. A positive edge indicates that, when one variable is present, the odds of another variable being present are higher, conditional on the remaining variables. A negative edge indicates lower conditional odds. An absent edge indicates that the association between two variables is not estimated as a direct association after accounting for the other variables in the network.

Psychological networks describe the conditional associations among variables within a psychological system. They are now a standard method in psychological science, with established procedures for estimation, accuracy assessment and reporting (Borsboom et al., 2021; Epskamp et al., 2018), and recent work has extended Ising estimation to Bayesian structure selection (Marsman et al., 2022). In education, psychological networks show how the components of learning and regulation relate to one another, rather than treating each component as a separate outcome (Saqr et al., 2024). Applications include self-regulation in academic writing (Saqr et al., 2021) and the relation between students’ monitoring events and the phases of regulation (Malmberg et al., 2022). Networks can also be estimated for a single learner, which shows how a process is organised within that person rather than assuming that the group-level network describes every student (Saqr & López-Pernas, 2024).

This article demonstrates how to estimate and interpret an Ising network using psychnets. The example uses five binary indicators of self-regulated learning. It explains how the estimated interactions can be interpreted, how node centrality and predictability can be examined, and how the regularized network can be compared with an unregularized estimator. The data are generated by a large language model and are used to illustrate the analysis rather than to draw conclusions about students.

library(psychnets)

The model

For a binary vector 𝐱∈{0,1}p\mathbf{x} \in \{0, 1\}^p, the Ising model gives

P(𝐱)=1Zexp⁡(∑iτixi+∑i<jωijxixj), P(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{Z}\exp\left(\sum_i \tau_i x_i + \sum_{i<j}\omega_{ij}x_i x_j\right),

where τi\tau_i is the threshold of node ii (its tendency to be 1 when all other nodes are 0), ωij\omega_{ij} the interaction between nodes ii and jj, and ZZ the normalizing constant. The conditional distribution of one node is a logistic regression on the others,

logit⁡P(Xi=1∣𝐗−i)=τi+∑j≠iωijXj, \operatorname{logit} P(X_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{X}_{-i}) = \tau_i + \sum_{j \ne i}\omega_{ij}X_j ,

so exp⁡(ωij)\exp(\omega_{ij}) is the conditional odds ratio of Xi=1X_i = 1 when XjX_j changes from 0 to 1.

The network is estimated by fitting a separate logistic regression for each node, using all remaining nodes as predictors. Each regression uses an ℓ1\ell_1 penalty, which shrinks coefficients and can set some of them to zero. The penalty is selected using the extended BIC with γ=0.25\gamma = 0.25. Because each pair of nodes appears in two regressions, the procedure produces two estimates for each possible interaction. The AND rule retains an edge only when both regressions select it, whereas the OR rule retains an edge when either regression selects it. For a retained edge, the two estimates are averaged to obtain its weight.

Data

SRL_GPT contains 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire. The responses were generated by a large language model (GPT) in a study examining how such models answer psychological surveys (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). They provide a structured example for demonstrating the analysis, but they do not represent observations from students. The construct scores are continuous. In this example, dichotomize() with method = "rank" converts each score into a binary indicator, coding a score as 1 when it falls in the upper half of its distribution and as 0 otherwise.

  • Nodes: five binary indicators, 1 for the upper half of CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value), SE (self-efficacy), SR (self-regulation) and TA (test anxiety).
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.
binary_data <- dichotomize(data = SRL_GPT, method = "rank")
head(binary_data)
#>      CSU IV SE SR TA
#> [1,]   0  0  0  0  1
#> [2,]   1  1  1  1  1
#> [3,]   1  1  1  1  0
#> [4,]   0  1  1  0  1
#> [5,]   0  0  0  0  1
#> [6,]   0  0  0  0  0
colMeans(binary_data)
#>       CSU        IV        SE        SR        TA 
#> 0.4966667 0.5366667 0.4766667 0.4600000 0.5000000

The proportion coded as 1 ranges from 46% to 54% across the five indicators. The proportions do not equal exactly 50% because tied scores remain on the same side of the split. Dichotomization reduces the information available in the original scores and should therefore be used only when the research question concerns the distinction between the two states. Variables that are naturally binary can be analysed without this additional step.

Which indicators are directly associated?

The function psychnet() estimates the network when method = "ising" is specified. The AND rule (rule = "AND") is the default and is stated explicitly here to make the estimation procedure clear.

ising_net <- psychnet(data = binary_data, method = "ising", rule = "AND")
summary(ising_net)
#> <psychnet> ising network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 6   (undirected)
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 2.53e-09
#>   edge weight: range [0.868, 2.201], mean 1.582
as.data.frame(ising_net)
#>   from to    weight
#> 1  CSU IV 2.0823827
#> 2  CSU SE 2.2005411
#> 3   IV SE 0.9297109
#> 4  CSU SR 0.8683591
#> 5   IV SR 2.1232839
#> 6   SE SR 1.2884921

The estimated network contains 6 edges, all positive and connecting the four learning constructs. Their weights range from 0.868 to 2.201. The strongest interaction is between CSU and SE (2.201). Conditional on the other indicators, being in the upper half of cognitive strategy use is associated with approximately nine times the odds of being in the upper half of self-efficacy (e2.201e^{2.201}). The weakest interaction is between CSU and SR (0.868), corresponding to an odds ratio of approximately 2.4.

Test anxiety has no estimated edge in this network. After accounting for the learning constructs, the model does not estimate a direct association between test anxiety and any of them. The Gaussian network estimated from the continuous scores contains a negative edge between self-regulation and test anxiety (-0.350; see the Gaussian graphical models article). The absence of this edge in the binary network illustrates how dichotomization can change the associations represented in a network by discarding information from the original scores.

Is the fitted network the optimum of its objective?

The penalized logistic regressions are solved iteratively. A solution to each regression must satisfy the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions. The certificate returned for the network is the largest violation of these conditions across the five regressions. A value close to zero indicates that the fitted solution satisfies the numerical optimality conditions of the objective.

certificate(ising_net)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1  ising 2.531323e-09  kkt      TRUE

The largest violation is 2.53×10−92.53 \times 10^{-9}, indicating that the fitted interactions satisfy the optimality conditions of the penalized regressions. This certificate assesses the numerical solution of the estimation procedure. It does not establish the sampling stability of the edges or the validity of the binary coding.

Which indicators are most connected?

The function net_centralities() returns two measures of node connectedness. Strength is the sum of the absolute interaction weights connected to a node, whereas expected influence is the sum of its signed interaction weights.

net_centralities(ising_net)
#>   node strength expected_influence
#> 1  CSU 5.151283           5.151283
#> 2   IV 5.135377           5.135377
#> 3   SE 4.418744           4.418744
#> 4   SR 4.280135           4.280135
#> 5   TA 0.000000           0.000000

Cognitive strategy use (5.151) and intrinsic value (5.135) have the highest strength, followed by self-efficacy (4.419) and self-regulation (4.280). Because all estimated edges are positive, expected influence has the same values as strength. Test anxiety has no edges and therefore has a value of 0 for both measures. The four learning indicators have similar levels of connectedness, while test anxiety is separated from them in the estimated network.

How well is each indicator classified from the others?

For a binary node, predictability describes how accurately its value can be classified using the other nodes in the network. The normalized classification coefficient (nCC) expresses this accuracy relative to the accuracy obtained by always predicting the more frequent category (Haslbeck & Waldorp, 2018):

nCC⁡j=CC⁡j−mj1−mj, \operatorname{nCC}_j = \frac{\operatorname{CC}_j - m_j}{1 - m_j},

where CC⁡j\operatorname{CC}_j is the proportion of correctly classified observations and mjm_j is the proportion belonging to the more frequent category. An nCC of 0 indicates no improvement over this base-rate prediction, while an nCC of 1 indicates perfect classification. net_predict() requires the original data to calculate predictability.

net_predict(ising_net, data = binary_data)
#>   node   type metric predictability  accuracy
#> 1  CSU binary    nCC      0.7114094 0.8566667
#> 2   IV binary    nCC      0.7338129 0.8766667
#> 3   SE binary    nCC      0.6993007 0.8566667
#> 4   SR binary    nCC      0.6376812 0.8333333
#> 5   TA binary    nCC      0.0000000 0.5000000

Intrinsic value has the highest predictability, with 87.7% of observations classified correctly and nCC = 0.734. Cognitive strategy use (nCC = 0.711) and self-efficacy (nCC = 0.699) follow, with 85.7% correct classification for each. Self-regulation has nCC = 0.638 and 83.3% correct classification. Test anxiety has nCC = 0 and 50% correct classification. Because it has no neighbours in the network, its classification is no better than the base-rate prediction. These values are calculated from the same data used to estimate the network and should be interpreted as in-sample results.

Does an unregularized estimator find the same network?

The estimator specified by method = "ising_sampler" fits the nodewise logistic regressions without a penalty. It then removes interactions whose Wald tests are not significant at the specified alpha level. Comparing this network with the regularized estimate allows us to examine whether the selected edge structure differs between the two estimation approaches.

unregularized_net <- psychnet(data = binary_data, method = "ising_sampler",
                              alpha = 0.05)
unregularized_net
#> <psychnet> ising_sampler network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 6   (undirected)
#>   optimality: unavailable
as.data.frame(unregularized_net)
#>   from to    weight
#> 1  CSU IV 2.2425237
#> 2  CSU SE 2.3454742
#> 3   IV SE 1.1870117
#> 4  CSU SR 0.8818853
#> 5   IV SR 2.2882117
#> 6   SE SR 1.4609560

The unregularized network contains the same 6 edges, and test anxiety remains isolated. The estimated interactions are larger than those in the regularized network. For example, the CSU–SE interaction is 2.345 rather than 2.201, and the IV–SR interaction is 2.288 rather than 2.123. This difference is consistent with the regularization procedure shrinking the estimated interactions. In this example, both estimators identify the same edge structure.

certificate(unregularized_net)
#>          method certificate kind certified
#> 1 ising_sampler          NA  kkt        NA

The certificate for the unregularized network is NA. The Wald pruning procedure sets non-significant interactions to zero, so the resulting network is no longer the maximum-likelihood solution for which the certificate evaluates the optimality conditions. The regularized network, in contrast, has a certified optimum.

What does the network look like?

The function cograph::splot() visualizes the network. Positive edges are shown in green and negative edges in red, while the ring around each node represents its predictability.

cograph::splot(ising_net, psych_styling = TRUE, predictability = TRUE)

The figure displays four learning indicators connected to one another and an isolated test anxiety node. The predictability ring for test anxiety is empty, reflecting its nCC of 0. Node positions are determined by the layout algorithm and do not have a statistical interpretation.

Reporting the analysis

A report of an Ising network should define what 1 and 0 represent for each node and explain how any dichotomization was performed. It should also state the sample size, estimator, value of γ\gamma, selection rule (AND or OR), and treatment of missing data. Interaction weights should be reported on the log-odds scale. Predictability should be reported using nCC alongside raw classification accuracy.

In this example, a regularized Ising network (γ=0.25\gamma = 0.25, AND rule) was estimated from rank-dichotomized scores for 300 complete responses. The network retained 6 positive edges among the learning constructs, with the largest interaction between CSU and SE (2.201), and test anxiety was isolated. An unregularized estimator with Wald pruning at 0.05 retained the same edges.

Assumptions and when to use the Ising model

  • The variables are binary. Ordinal or continuous variables should not be dichotomized only to fit the model, since the example shows that a median split can remove a substantive edge.
  • Observations are independent of one another.
  • The nodewise regressions of a pair can disagree. The AND rule gives a sparser and more conservative network, the OR rule a denser one; edges that appear only under OR should be reported as rule-dependent.
  • For networks that combine binary and continuous variables, use a mixed graphical model.
  • Edges are conditional associations, not causal effects.
